newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarians vote with eyes on IMF mission.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarians vote with eyes on IMF mission.

text.p: Bulgarians frustrated by deep economic crisis look set to elect anti-communist opposition candidate Petar Stoyanov in Sunday's second round of presidential elections.

But the key to the Balkan country's recovery lies less with the president than with an International Monetary Fund mission discussing terms for release of a $115 million credit vital to prevent Bulgaria defaulting on its foreign debt.
The candidate of the governing Socialists, Culture Minister Ivan Marazov, lagged 17 points behind Stoyanov in last Sunday's first round.
Many votes went to protest candidates and turnout is expected to be lower than the first round's 63 percent.
Opinion polls give Stoyanov between 57 and 64 percent of the vote, comfortably ahead of his rival, but many Bulgarians are disillusioned with politicians of any colour.
"I just don't know how I am going to support my family this winter," said Vladimir Grancharov, a civil servant in his 40s.
Neighbouring Romania and Yugoslavia, also voting on Sunday, are themselves battling economic crisis. But Bulgaria, a laggard in reform, has the lowest foreign investment in the region.

Stoyanov, an advocate of a market economy and closer ties with the European Union and NATO, received enthusiastic backing from students at a Friday rally as he repeated his call for an acceleration of long-delayed reforms.

Marazov, an art historian, courted mostly elderly Socialist Party supporters at his last election rally with an appeal for stability and pledges to revive Bulgaria's communist-era trade links with Russia and other former Soviet republics.

The maverick populist head of the Bulgarian Business Bloc, George Ganchev, won the lion's share of protest votes last week, polling 21.8 percent. He has declined to back either second round candidate.
Under Bulgaria's post-communist constitution the president is a largely ceremonial figure and real power lies with parliament where Prime Minister Zhan Videnov's Socialists have a clear majority.
Party reformists predict a split after the elections which could lead to parliamentary elections.
IMF mission leader Anne McGuirk, who is due to meet Videnov on Sunday, told reporters the Fund would evaluate Bulgaria's reform performance before deciding on further funding.
The IMF has twice postponed the $115 million second tranche of its standby credit, saying the government must fulfil its pledges to close loss-making state enterprises and speed up privatisation.

In a last-minute bid to convince the Fund of its commitment to reform, the Bulgarian National Bank on Thursday started bankruptcy proceedings for eight out of nine banks placed in receivership in September.

Economic austerity and the threat of bread and fuel shortages in the coming winter have thrown a shadow over an election campaign already marred by bombings and violence culminating in the October 2 assassination of former prime minister Andrei Lukanov.
On Wednesday a home-made bomb destroyed the car of Haralambi Anchev, a member of the Central Electoral Committee.
